entries: It is a task to come to see the world as it is.
Iris Murdoch, The Sovereignty of Good, The Sovereignty of Good Over Other Concepts, p. 89 (Routledge, 2014)
Philosophy
Corrected: the sentence stands on page 89 of the Routledge edition of 2014. The proposal cited page 91 of the 1970 printing, which was never opened.
What we see there are not giants but windmills, and what seem to be their arms are the sails that turned by the wind make the millstone go.
Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part I, ch. VIII (Sancho Panza) (trans. John Ormsby, 1885)
Fiction

Corrected wording: Ormsby breaks the speech with a narrative tag, so the address and the sentence are not one sentence on the page. The sentence ships alone, word for word, with a capital at the head.
O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as others see us!
Robert Burns, To a Louse, final stanza, lines 1 to 2, Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect (Kilmarnock, 1786)
Poetry

Corrected against the 1786 Kilmarnock text. The proposal read Power and ithers. Both the Kilmarnock edition and the Edinburgh edition of 1787 print Pow’r and others, so the line ships as Burns published it.

I ask no favors for my sex. I surrender not our claim to equality. All I ask of our brethren is, that they will take their feet from off our necks, and permit us to stand upright on that ground which God designed us to occupy.
Sarah Moore Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, Letter II, to Mary S. Parker, 7th mo. 17, 1837 (Isaac Knapp, 1838)
Correspondence
Corrected: in the Isaac Knapp text of 1838 the printed sentence opens with the word But. The quotation begins at I, so that one conjunction is dropped and nothing else is altered.
The words of truth are naturally simple, and justice needs no subtle interpretations, for it has a fitness in itself; but the words of injustice, being sick in themselves, require clever treatment.
Euripides, The Phoenician Women, line 469 (Polyneices) (trans. E. P. Coleridge, 1938)
Drama
If this book be not the exact, the absolute, the strict truth, it has no right to exist.
Marie Bashkirtseff, The Journal of Marie Bashkirtseff, Author’s Preface (trans. Mathilde Blind, 1890)
Diary
We ought not to be ashamed of appreciating the truth and of acquiring it wherever it comes from, even if it comes from races distant and nations different from us.
Al-Kindi, On First Philosophy, p. 58 (trans. Alfred L. Ivry, 1974)
Philosophy
Transparence means experiencing the luminousness of the thing in itself, of things being what they are.
Susan Sontag, Against Interpretation, section 9, in Against Interpretation and Other Essays (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1966)
Essay
Why can’t I tell the true shape of Lu-shan? / Because I myself am in the mountain.
Su Shi, Written on the Wall at West Forest Temple, 1084, closing couplet (trans. attributed to Burton Watson, 1994)
Poetry
Hedged: no printed copy was opened. Two secondary witnesses give this wording exactly and a third differs, so the translator is named as attributed and no page is printed.
‘But he hasn’t got anything on,’ a little child said.
Hans Christian Andersen, The Emperor’s New Clothes, at the procession near the close (trans. Jean Hersholt, 1949)
Fiction
The truth is rarely pure and never simple.
Oscar Wilde, The Importance of Being Earnest, First Act (Algernon Moncrieff)
Drama
We know truth, not only by the reason, but also by the heart, and it is in this last way that we know first principles; and reason, which has no part in it, tries in vain to impugn them.
Blaise Pascal, Pensées, Section IV, Of the Means of Belief, no. 282 (trans. W. F. Trotter, 1910)
Philosophy

To have some account of my thoughts, manners, acquaintance and actions, when the hour arrives in which time is more nimble than memory, is the reason which induces me to keep a Journal. A Journal in which I must confess my every thought, must open my whole heart!
Frances Burney, The Early Diary of Frances Burney, the first entry, Poland Street, 27 March 1768 (ed. Annie Raine Ellis, 1889)
Diary

Earth’s crammed with heaven, / And every common bush afire with God: / But only he who sees, takes off his shoes, / The rest sit round it, and pluck blackberries, / And daub their natural faces unaware / More and more, from the first similitude.
Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Aurora Leigh, Seventh Book, first edition of 1857 (Aurora)
Poetry
Corrected against the page images of the first edition of 1857, which sets a comma after takes off his shoes where the proposal had a semicolon. The lines are Aurora’s own narration.
I do not enjoy making ‘desolation,’ believe me, but I cannot change my eyes!
Gustave Flaubert, letter CCCI to George Sand, December 1875, The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters (trans. Aimée L. McKenzie, 1921)
Correspondence
yes I said yes I will Yes.
James Joyce, Ulysses, episode 18, Penelope, closing words (Molly Bloom)
Fiction
There is no department of inquiry in which it is not full as easy to miss truth as to find it, even when the materials from which truth is to be drawn are actually present to our senses.
Harriet Martineau, How to Observe: Morals and Manners, Part I, Introduction, the opening sentence (Charles Knight, 1838)
Philosophy
This book was written in good faith, reader.
Michel de Montaigne, Essays, To the Reader, the opening sentence (trans. Donald M. Frame, 1957)
Essay
It is this, let me tell you—that the strongest man in the world is he who stands most alone.
Henrik Ibsen, An Enemy of the People, Act V, his last speech (Dr. Stockmann) (trans. R. Farquharson Sharp, 1911)
Drama
Corrected: this is Dr. Stockmann’s last speech, not the closing words of the play. Two short speeches follow it, and Petra has the final word. The wording is verified in Farquharson Sharp.
Myself when young did eagerly frequent / Doctor and Saint, and heard great Argument / About it and about: but evermore / Came out by the same Door as in I went.
Omar Khayyám, Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, quatrain XXVII, first edition (trans. Edward FitzGerald, 1859)
Poetry
And in fact I did cut it in punishment for such stupidity: for there seemed to me no cause for a head to be adorned with hair and naked of learning—which was the more desired embellishment.
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Response to Sor Filotea (1691), in Poems, Protest, and a Dream, p. 15 (trans. Margaret Sayers Peden, 1997)
Correspondence
Corrected: the work is named Response to Sor Filotea, and these words close a longer sentence, so the opening capital is the card’s. The page rests on one secondary citation.
To see what is in front of one’s nose needs a constant struggle.
George Orwell, In Front of Your Nose, Tribune, 22 March 1946, penultimate paragraph
Essay
To experience means to know facts just as they are, to know in accordance with facts by completely relinquishing one’s own fabrications.
Nishida Kitarō, An Inquiry into the Good, Part I, ch. 1, the opening sentence (trans. Masao Abe and Christopher Ives, 1990)
Philosophy
Corrected: an earlier reading cut the sentence at they are and closed it with a stop the book does not have. The whole sentence ships, as every witness prints it.
My apologies to great questions for small answers.
Wisława Szymborska, Under One Small Star, in View with a Grain of Sand, p. 91 (trans. Stanisław Barańczak and Clare Cavanagh, 1995)
Poetry
Corrected: the edition and the year. The line stands verbatim on page 91 of View with a Grain of Sand, Harcourt, 1995, where this rendering first appeared.
The question is not what you look at, but what you see.
Henry David Thoreau, Journal, entry of 5 August 1851, vol. II, p. 373 (ed. Bradford Torrey, 1906)
Diary
Corrected: the Journal volume of 1906 names Bradford Torrey alone as its editor, not Torrey with Francis H. Allen, who joined the edition later. The volume and page are added.
We live close together and we live far apart.
Susan Glaspell, Trifles, the one act, near the close, in Plays (1920) (Mrs Hale)
Drama
How odd it is that every one should not see that all observation must be for or against some view, if it is to be of any service.
Charles Darwin, letter to Henry Fawcett, 18 September 1861, Darwin Correspondence Project letter 3257
Correspondence
Hundreds of people can talk for one who can think, but thousands can think for one who can see. To see clearly is poetry, prophecy, and religion,—all in one.
John Ruskin, Modern Painters, Volume III, Part IV, ch. XVI, Of Modern Landscape, section 28 (1856)
Essay
Every man takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world.
Arthur Schopenhauer, Studies in Pessimism, Further Psychological Observations (trans. T. Bailey Saunders, 1890)
Philosophy
I shall be employed about things, not words!
Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, the Introduction (1792)
Essay

unused.quote: I was always embarrassed by the words sacred, glorious, and sacrifice and the expression in vain.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, A Farewell to Arms, Book III, chapter 27 (Frederic Henry) (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1929)
unused.note: Verified in the Scribner text of 1929 and attacked without a mark on it. Held only because one Hemingway can stand in a month and two are already carried.

unused.quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts.
unused.source: Mark Twain, The Innocents Abroad, Conclusion (1869)
unused.note: Verified in the Conclusion of 1869. A travel line more than a truth line, so it belongs to a travelling month.

unused.quote: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own, chapter 1 (1929)
unused.note: Verified. The Woolf Society lists the eat well variant as the false one and this think well wording as the true one.

unused.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
unused.source: Italo Calvino, Why Read the Classics?, definition 6, The New York Review of Books, 9 October 1986 (trans. Patrick Creagh, 1986)
unused.note: Verified in Creagh’s rendering of 1986. A reading line, so it wants a month about books.

unused.quote: I am in fact a Hobbit (in all but size).
unused.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Letters of J. R. R. Tolkien, letter 213, to Deborah Webster, 25 October 1958 (ed. Humphrey Carpenter, 1981)
unused.note: Verified in letter 213 of the Carpenter edition. A self knowledge line with a homely turn.

unused.quote: Men may dyen of ymaginacioun, / So depe may impressioun be take.
unused.source: Geoffrey Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Miller’s Tale, lines 3612 to 3613, The Riverside Chaucer (the Miller)
unused.note: Verified in the Riverside lineation. Middle English on the page, which suits a month with room for older spelling.

unused.quote: Give me Books, fruit, French wine and fine weather and a little music out of doors, played by somebody I do not know.
unused.source: John Keats, Letters of John Keats to His Family and Friends, letter CXIII to Fanny Keats, 28 August 1819 (ed. Sidney Colvin, 1891)
unused.note: Corrected to Colvin’s wording, which the circulating version reorders. The full stop is the card’s because the sentence runs on.

unused.quote: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
unused.source: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Proverbs of Hell, the tenth proverb (1790)
unused.note: Verified as the tenth Proverb of Hell. Eternity and time, so it reads as a closing year line.

unused.quote: All letters, methinks, should be free and easy as one’s discourse; not studied as an oration, nor made up of hard words like a charm.
unused.source: Dorothy Osborne, Letters from Dorothy Osborne to Sir William Temple, Letter 33, pp. 160 to 161 (ed. Edward Abbott Parry, 1888)
unused.note: Corrected to Letter 33 in Parry’s edition of 1888, running across pages 160 and 161. The undated heading is kept as Parry prints it.

unused.quote: I hope it is no very cynical asperity not to confess obligations where no benefit has been received, or to be unwilling that the Publick should consider me as owing that to a Patron, which Providence has enabled me to do for myself.
unused.source: Samuel Johnson, letter to Lord Chesterfield, 7 February 1755, in Boswell, Life of Johnson, under 1755
unused.note: Corrected to the wording Boswell prints, with obligations in the plural and Publick in the old spelling. The manuscript behind the Hyde edition differs again.

unused.quote: I’ll make my report as if I told a story, for I was taught as a child on my homeworld that Truth is a matter of the imagination.
unused.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness, chapter 1, opening sentence (Genly Ai)
unused.note: Verified as the first sentence of Genly Ai’s report. Truth as a matter of the imagination, which is a strong line for any month about story.

unused.quote: To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.
unused.source: Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious, in Labyrinths, closing pages (trans. James E. Irby, 1962)
unused.note: Verified in Irby’s Labyrinths after a refutation sent it back. The Kerrigan wording is a different rendering of the same close.

unused.quote: He could see plainly that she was not herself. That is, he could not see that she was becoming herself and daily casting aside that fictitious self which we assume like a garment with which to appear before the world.
unused.source: Kate Chopin, The Awakening, chapter XIX (1899)
unused.note: Verified in chapter XIX of 1899. Casting aside the fictitious self, which is a truth line held for want of a day.

unused.quote: Good prose is like a window pane.
unused.source: George Orwell, Why I Write, the final paragraph (Gangrel, No. 4, Summer 1946)
unused.note: Verified in the final paragraph of Gangrel, Summer 1946. Held because Orwell can stand once in a month.

unused.quote: I wished to tell the truth, for truth always conveys its own moral to those who are able to receive it.
unused.source: Anne Brontë, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, Preface to the Second Edition, 22 July 1848
unused.note: Verified in the Preface to the second edition of 1848. A plain statement of purpose.

unused.quote: The writer should never be ashamed of staring. There is nothing that doesn’t require his attention.
unused.source: Flannery O’Connor, Mystery and Manners, The Nature and Aim of Fiction (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1969)
unused.note: Verified in Mystery and Manners. Attention as a discipline, which suits a month about looking.

unused.quote: God offers to every mind its choice between truth and repose.
unused.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Intellect, essay XI in Essays: First Series (1841)
unused.note: Verified in essay XI of Essays: First Series. Truth or repose, and the choice is the whole line.

unused.quote: Conceptually, we may call truth what we cannot change; metaphorically, it is the ground on which we stand and the sky that stretches above us.
unused.source: Hannah Arendt, Truth and Politics, in Between Past and Future, closing sentence, p. 264 (Viking, 1968)
unused.note: Verified as the closing sentence of Truth and Politics. Held because the month was already full of ground and sky.

unused.quote: The public must decide whether it wishes to continue on the present road, and it can do so only when in full possession of the facts.
unused.source: Rachel Carson, Silent Spring, chapter 2, The Obligation to Endure (Houghton Mifflin, 1962)
unused.note: Verified in chapter 2 of Silent Spring. Full possession of the facts, a public truth line.

unused.quote: We are learning that a standard of social ethics is not attained by travelling a sequestered byway, but by mixing on the thronged and common road where all must turn out for one another, and at least see the size of one another’s burdens.
unused.source: Jane Addams, Democracy and Social Ethics, chapter I, Introduction (Macmillan, 1902)
unused.note: Verified in the Introduction of 1902. Seeing the size of one another’s burdens, which is sympathy more than clarity.

unused.quote: He that would seriously set upon the search of truth, ought in the first place to prepare his mind with a love of it.
unused.source: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book IV, ch. XIX, Of Enthusiasm, section 1 (ed. Fraser, 1894, vol. II, p. 428)
unused.note: Corrected against Fraser’s Clarendon edition of 1894, which keeps the comma after truth. Of Enthusiasm was added in the fourth edition of 1700.

unused.quote: Untruth naturally afflicts historical information.
unused.source: Ibn Khaldun, The Muqaddimah, the opening of Book One of the Kitab al-Ibar (trans. Franz Rosenthal, 1958)
unused.note: Corrected to the opening of Book One of the Kitab al Ibar after a refutation showed Rosenthal keeps the Introduction apart. No page is printed because none was opened.

unused.quote: Freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently.
unused.source: Rosa Luxemburg, The Russian Revolution, ch. 6, The Problem of Dictatorship (trans. Bertram D. Wolfe, 1940)
unused.note: Verified in Wolfe’s translation of 1940. Freedom for the one who thinks differently, a line about dissent.

unused.quote: My way of joking is to tell the truth. It’s the funniest joke in the world.
unused.source: Bernard Shaw, John Bull’s Other Island, Act II, his reply to Nora Reilly (Peter Keegan)
unused.note: Verified as Peter Keegan’s reply to Nora Reilly. Held because the drama lane was already full.

unused.quote: Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?
unused.source: Thornton Wilder, Our Town, Act III, the graveyard scene (Emily)
unused.note: Corrected to the graveyard scene and to Emily, since in Act III she is married. No edition was opened, so the reading rests on eight published books.

unused.quote: I’m nobody! Who are you? / Are you nobody, too?
unused.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘I’m nobody! Who are you?’, Poems, Second Series, Life I, lines 1 to 2 (Roberts Brothers, 1891)
unused.note: Verified in Poems, Second Series of 1891. Two lines only, in that edition’s lineation.

unused.quote: I, too, dislike it.
unused.source: Marianne Moore, Poetry, line 1, Complete Poems (Macmillan and Viking, 1967)
unused.note: Corrected to the three line final text of 1967, because the printings of 1919 and 1924 read I too, dislike it with one comma.

unused.quote: The universe is made of stories, / not of atoms.
unused.source: Muriel Rukeyser, The Speed of Darkness, section IX (Random House, 1968)
unused.note: Verified in section IX of The Speed of Darkness. Stories rather than atoms, a line about what the world is made of.

unused.quote: The door itself / makes no promises. / It is only a door.
unused.source: Adrienne Rich, Prospective Immigrants Please Note, closing lines, Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law (Harper and Row, 1963)
unused.note: Corrected publisher: Harper and Row published the book in 1963 and Norton reissued it in 1967.

unused.quote: Although the wind / blows terribly here, / the moonlight also leaks / between the roof planks / of this ruined house.
unused.source: Izumi Shikibu, The Ink Dark Moon, the poem beginning ‘Although the wind’ (trans. Jane Hirshfield with Mariko Aratani, 1988)
unused.note: Verified in Hirshfield and Aratani of 1988. Five lines in that edition’s lineation.

unused.quote: I am large, I contain multitudes.
unused.source: Walt Whitman, Leaves of Grass, ‘Song of Myself’, section 51, 1881 text
unused.note: Verified; parenthetical in the source. Not a beginning line so much as a truth-and-clarity line.

unused.quote: We tell ourselves stories in order to live.
unused.source: Joan Didion, The White Album, the title essay, opening sentence (Simon and Schuster, 1979)
unused.note: Verified opening line. The essay goes on to test the claim, so the line is cooler than it reads alone; a truth-and-clarity line.

unused.quote: Never did eye see the sun unless it had first become sunlike, and never can the soul have vision of the First Beauty unless itself be beautiful.
unused.source: Plotinus, Enneads, I.6.9, On Beauty (trans. Stephen MacKenna, 1917)
unused.note: Verified in MacKenna 1917. A clarity line rather than a beginning line.

unused.quote: The greatest benefit we owe to the artist, whether painter, poet, or novelist, is the extension of our sympathies.
unused.source: George Eliot, The Natural History of German Life, Westminster Review, July 1856; in Essays of George Eliot, ed. Sheppard (1883), essay V
unused.note: Verified twice in the Sheppard edition; refuted only as a month collision with the Middlemarch line, which landed. Eliot stands at two for the year after February.

unused.quote: Some men say an army of horse and some men say an army on foot and some men say an army of ships is the most beautiful thing on the black earth. But I say it is what you love.
unused.source: Sappho, If Not, Winter, Fragment 16, lines 1 to 4 (trans. Anne Carson, 2002)
unused.note: Carried from January, verified in Carson, p. 27. Before it lands, the four lines must be marked with slashes in Carson’s lineation, which nobody has yet checked against the page; it is carried as prose.

unused.quote: For to be possessed of a vigorous mind is not enough; the prime requisite is rightly to apply it.
unused.source: René Descartes, Discourse on the Method, Part I, first paragraph (trans. John Veitch, 1850)
unused.note: Verified in Veitch; the 1850 date is from memory, not from a scan. Right application of the mind: a clarity line.

unused.quote: Travel is in my opinion a very profitable exercise; the soul is there continually employed in observing new and unknown things, and I do not know, as I have often said a better school wherein to model life than by incessantly exposing to it the diversity of so many other lives, fancies, and usances, and by making it relish a perpetual variety of forms of human nature.
unused.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book III, ch. 9, Of Vanity (trans. Charles Cotton, revised by W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)
unused.note: Verified. Another Montaigne is already held for May, so this goes on to the month of clear seeing.

unused.quote: You can’t get away from yourself by moving from one place to another.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book I, chapter 2 (Jake Barnes)
unused.note: Verified, Jake to Robert Cohn. It corrects the traveller rather than sending him out, so it reads as a truth line and not an April line.

unused.quote: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
unused.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 5.6 (trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922)
unused.note: Verified. Held because Wittgenstein can appear once in a month and proposition 7 is the stronger line for a quieter month.

unused.quote: Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty.
unused.source: David Hume, Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, Of the Standard of Taste (ed. Miller, pp. 229 to 230)
unused.note: Corrected in re-verification. Held: Hume sets the sentence out as the sceptical case and the next paragraph restrains it, so it wants a month about seeing clearly.

unused.quote: The problem in public life is learning to overcome terror; the problem in married life is learning to overcome boredom.
unused.source: Gabriel García Márquez, Love in the Time of Cholera, chapter 4 (Fermina Daza) (trans. Edith Grossman, 1988)
unused.note: Corrected: the sentence is Fermina Daza’s own. Held: it is plain speech about two kinds of life rather than counsel.

unused.quote: Man is least himself when he talks in his own person. Give him a mask, and he will tell you the truth.
unused.source: Oscar Wilde, The Critic as Artist, Part II, in Intentions, 1891 (Gilbert)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the mask line is about how truth gets said, so it wants the month of plain speech.

unused.quote: The most exhausting thing in life, I have discovered, is being insincere.
unused.source: Anne Morrow Lindbergh, Gift from the Sea, chapter 2, Channelled Whelk (1955)
unused.note: Hedged: Gift from the Sea was never opened and the reference readings agree on chapter 2. Held for a month about sincerity.

unused.quote: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
unused.source: Francis Bacon, Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Of Studies (1625)
unused.note: Verified. Held only because Bacon lands in May with Read not to contradict; one person a month.

unused.quote: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
unused.source: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, chapter II, Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion (1859)
unused.note: Verified. Held: knowing both sides is the discipline of clear seeing, which is June’s ground.

unused.quote: All men by nature desire to know.
unused.source: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book I, ch. 1, 980a21 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1908)
unused.note: Verified opening of the Metaphysics. Held: all men by nature desire to know is the appetite for truth.

unused.quote: I did not care what it was all about. All I wanted to know was how to live in it. Maybe if you found out how to live in it you learned from that what it was all about.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book II, chapter 14 (Jake Barnes) (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1926)
unused.note: Verified in the Scribner text of 1926. Held: Jake wants to know how to live in it, which is a search for clarity.

unused.quote: I can resist everything except temptation.
unused.source: Oscar Wilde, Lady Windermere’s Fan, First Act (Lord Darlington)
unused.note: Verified, First Act. Held: the inversion is wit about self-knowledge and the play rebukes it in the next line.

unused.quote: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, Mrs Dalloway, the opening sentence (1925)
unused.note: Verified opening line. Held: Mrs Dalloway buying the flowers herself is plain speech about a whole life, and it offers no counsel.

unused.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
unused.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
unused.note: Corrected: the sentence is in The Return, Part II. Held: it is the traveller only that is foreign is a correction of the eye, which is June.

report.thinnestLane: Diary: three survivors in the whole pool and all three used, so a rerun on shortfall would have to go there first
